note: The voiceover script for the tour video, one line per tour step (same order as src/tour.js). Read by Kokoro, an open-source voice (code MIT, model Apache 2.0).
lines: Meet The RM Assistant: one AI assistant for every relationship manager. It finds the clients worth calling, prepares each meeting, and writes the follow-up.
You're Jordan Ellis, a senior relationship manager with twelve business clients. Everything here is sample data.
Each Monday starts here: the clients worth a call this week, and every number checked against its source.
First, the Signal Finder runs plain rules the business owns, like idle cash or check fraud exposure. It also reads real Federal Reserve rate data.
Then Claude explains each one in plain English, with talking points and a next step, using only the numbers behind it.
Before Jordan can use a draft, every number is checked against the data. Anything that can't be traced is flagged.
Jordan decides: use it, change it, or reject it. Using it creates an opportunity tagged as AI-sourced, so the results can be counted.
Before Tuesday's meeting, the assistant looks up four sources on its own, and shows every step it took.
The result is a one-page brief, with a source on every fact.
After the meeting, it drafts the recap, the email, and the CRM call note. There's no recording without the client's consent, so it works from Jordan's notes.
Nothing is saved or sent until Jordan approves. Anything unclear comes back marked check, instead of guessed.
Try to break it. Ask for a credit decision, a price, or another banker's client, and the guardrails stop it before any AI sees it.
Five measures from day one: usage, quality, business impact, adoption, and risk. A pilot compares bankers who have the assistant with bankers who don't.
A pilot needs access to client data, a risk partner from day one, and a small group of relationship managers. Our assumption, to confirm: data access sets the pace.
Now it's your turn. Run the agents live on Claude, from any screen.
